content: The NDUFB7 protein, also referred to as NADH dehydrogenase 1 beta subcomplex subunit 7 or Complex I-B18, is an enzyme encoded by the NDUFB7 gene in humans. This protein is an accessory subunit of the NADH dehydrogenase (ubiquinone) complex, which is located in the inner mitochondrial membrane. It is also known as Complex I, the largest of the five complexes that constitute the electron transport chain. The NDUFB7 protein is 6,000 base pairs long, has a molecular weight of approximately 4 kDa, and consists of 137 amino acids. It is a subunit of the NADH dehydrogenase (ubiquinone) enzyme, which is the largest respiratory complex. Structurally, the enzyme is L-shaped, with a long hydrophobic transmembrane domain and a hydrophilic domain that forms the peripheral arm. This peripheral arm contains all the known redox centers and the NADH binding site. Both NDUFB7 and NDUFB8 are localized at the intermembrane surface of Complex I. The N-terminal hydrophobic domain of NDUFB7 has the potential to fold into an alpha-helix that spans the inner mitochondrial membrane, while the C-terminal hydrophilic domain interacts with the globular subunits of Complex I. The highly conserved two-domain structure of NDUFB7 suggests that this feature is critical for its function. The hydrophobic domain likely serves as an anchor for the NADH dehydrogenase (ubiquinone) complex within the inner mitochondrial membrane. The protein encoded by the NDUFB7 gene is an accessory subunit of the multisubunit NADH:ubiquinone oxidoreductase (Complex I). This subunit is not directly involved in the catalytic activity of the enzyme. Mammalian Complex I is composed of 45 distinct subunits and is located in the inner mitochondrial membrane. The protein complex exhibits NADH dehydrogenase and oxidoreductase activities, transferring electrons from NADH to the respiratory chain. The immediate electron acceptor for this enzyme is believed to be ubiquinone. Alternative splicing occurs at the NDUFB7 locus, resulting in two transcript variants that encode distinct isoforms. The electron transfer process begins when NADH binds to Complex I and donates two electrons to the isoalloxazine ring of the flavin mononucleotide (FMN) prosthetic group, forming FMNH2. These electrons are then transferred through a series of iron-sulfur (Fe-S) clusters within the prosthetic arm and ultimately to coenzyme Q10 (CoQ), which is reduced to ubiquinol (CoQH2). The flow of electrons through Complex I alters the redox state of the protein, inducing a conformational change and a shift in the pK of ionizable side chains. This process drives the pumping of four hydrogen ions (protons) out of the mitochondrial matrix, contributing to the generation of the proton gradient required for ATP synthesis.
